beats.care: Parents and grandparents are prime targets. Tell them real police never arrest anyone on a video call or ask for money transfers.
beats.what: Scammers posing as CBI officers video-called a 72-year-old woman in Nampally and got her to transfer ₹2.20 crore as so-called security deposits.
beats.why: They claimed a parcel with drugs was booked in her name, showed a fake arrest warrant, and kept her scared until she paid.

cards.body: It's a scam, not a law. Fraudsters pose as police, CBI or customs, accuse you of a crime, and keep you on a video call for hours so you can't check with anyone. Then they demand money to 'clear your name'.
cards.title: what is a 'digital arrest'?

cards.body: Hyderabad City Police issued a public advisory against digital arrest calls this week. If you're targeted, hang up and report at 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in. Reporting fast gives the best chance of freezing the money.
The scammers called the transfers 'security deposits', making a theft sound like an official legal step.

cards.q: What's the biggest red flag in a 'digital arrest' call?
cards.why: Real agencies never arrest you or collect money over a video call, so that demand means it's a scam.

hook: A video call, a fake CBI officer, *₹2.20 crore gone*. Spot the trick

learn.t: 'Digital arrest' isn't a real legal process: no police or agency arrests you or collects money over a video call.
